name: Timeline Pattern Analysis
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Connecting the Dots: Four Decades on One Timeline
lesson.summary: Laying the field's major milestones end to end, from Feynman's 1981 proposal to the still-unrealized ROI of 2025, reveals a repeating structure of breakthrough, reinterpretation, and quiet goalpost-moving.
lesson.body:
Individually, each milestone in quantum computing's history looks like solid, incremental progress. Richard Feynman's 1981 talk proposing that quantum systems be simulated by other quantum systems was a genuine conceptual breakthrough. Peter Shor's 1994 factoring algorithm was a real and still-unmatched piece of theoretical computer science. The first laboratory demonstrations between 1998 and 2001, culminating in a widely reported experiment where a small number of qubits factored the number 15 into 3 times 5, were real physical achievements. D-Wave's 2007 announcement of a commercial machine, Google's 2019 Sycamore claim, and IBM's 2023 Condor chip were all real engineering events. Laid out individually, they read as a steady march forward.

Laid end to end on a single timeline, though, a different pattern emerges. Each milestone was accompanied, at the time, by predictions that practical, world-changing quantum computers were close, typically framed as a three-to-five-year horizon. Feynman's 1981 idea inspired physicists who, by the 1990s, were predicting working machines within a decade. Shor's 1994 algorithm triggered urgency, particularly from cryptographers, about encryption being broken within years, not decades. The 1998 to 2001 lab demos were reported with language suggesting rapid follow-on scaling. D-Wave's 2007 launch was marketed as commercial quantum computing having arrived. Google's 2019 supremacy claim was widely read as a threshold after which practical advantage would follow quickly. IBM's roadmap through Condor in 2023 kept that same near-term promise alive. Each time, the predicted horizon slid forward again once the milestone passed.

This is not evidence of dishonesty so much as a structural feature of how frontier science gets communicated. Researchers close to a hard problem tend to see the remaining obstacles as solvable in principle, which gets compressed, by the time it reaches press releases and investor decks, into solvable soon. The scientists behind each milestone were not lying; many described genuine technical progress accurately in their own papers. The distortion happens at the interface between careful technical claims and the narrative built on top of them, a distinction worth holding onto as the next chapters catalog specific instances of this gap.

The 2025 result of essentially zero commercial ROI, discussed in the previous chapter, is the most recent data point on this same timeline, and it fits the pattern rather than breaking it. Every prior milestone was followed by continued NISQ-era limitations rather than the leap to fault tolerance that headlines implied was imminent. Recognizing this as a pattern, rather than a series of unrelated disappointments, is the analytical tool this chapter introduces, and it is the tool the rest of this unit applies to specific recurring claims: the three-to-five-year horizon that keeps resetting, the roughly forty-year arc since Feynman, and the catalog of specific broken promises that pattern produced.

None of this implies quantum computing is fraudulent or worthless. Genuine hardware progress, measured in qubit counts, gate fidelities, and error rates, has been real and roughly continuous since the 1990s. What the pattern shows is that the rate of progress toward practical usefulness has been consistently overstated in public communication relative to the rate of progress in the underlying engineering, and that gap is wide enough, and repeats often enough, to be treated as a structural feature of the field rather than a series of coincidences.
